title: Moses goes out and sees (Exodus 2:11–15)
hook: the prince goes out to his people and sees their burdens

segments.voice: Yesterday, tevah, the basket on the Nile: a mother let go, a sister watched, a princess drew him out. Your line was someone watches the basket. Now the baby is a grown man, raised in a palace. Day eighty.

Some people grow up very close to suffering, and never see it. They drive past the same streets every day. The people who clean their houses, cook their food, build their buildings, are right there, and somehow invisible. Moses grew up in Pharaoh's palace. He had food, clothes, and a princess for a mother. Just outside, his own people were making bricks under the whip. He could have lived his whole life without looking. The Torah skips his entire childhood in a single verse. Then it says: when Moses had grown up, he went out. Today: what happens when he does.
screen: `RIGHT THERE, AND INVISIBLE.` → `A PRINCE IN PHARAOH'S PALACE.` → `ONE DAY, HE WENT OUT.`

segments.voice: The verse is short, and every word counts: "he went out unto his brethren, and looked on their burdens." His brethren. He knows who they are. He's not a tourist. And he looked on their burdens. The midrash takes that word looked very seriously. It says Moses didn't just glance. He saw their loads and wept. He'd put his own shoulder under the bricks to help, one person at a time. Then he sees something worse: an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his brethren. And the text slows down: he looked this way and that way, and saw there was no man. And he struck the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand. The Torah doesn't praise it, and doesn't condemn it. The rabbis read that look in different ways. Some say he looked to be sure no one would see. Others say he looked to see whether anyone else would step in, and there was no one; so he did. The next day he goes out again, and sees two Hebrews fighting each other. He tries to stop them, and one turns on him: "Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?" Are you going to kill me too? The secret is out. Pharaoh hears, and wants him dead, and Moses runs, all the way to Midian. And there, sitting by a well, what does he do? He sees shepherds pushing some young women away from the water, and he stands up and helps them. He can't stop seeing. That's the first thing we learn about the man who will lead the Exodus. Before any miracles. He went out, and he saw.
screen: `HE LOOKED ON THEIR BURDENS.` · `THIS WAY AND THAT, AND NO ONE.` · `WHO MADE THEE A RULER OVER US?` · `AT THE WELL, HE STILL SEES.` · then, large: `HE WENT OUT AND SAW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look straight at one hard reality. Settle, and breathe. Think of a burden someone near you carries that's easy not to see. Someone you pass every day on the way to work. A neighbor who's struggling. People in your own city living a very different life than yours. Don't solve it. Don't look away either. Just see it, honestly, for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Vayar, Hebrew for and he saw, the verb that runs through this whole story. A prince who leaves the palace, looks at his people's burdens, and can't look away.
Your line: he went out and saw. Today, look for one burden you usually walk past, and actually see the person carrying it. Day eighty.

howItsDone: Jewish teachers often point to this passage as the first sign of Moses' leadership: before God speaks to him, he goes out to his people and sees their suffering.

fork.setup: you're Moses, a prince of Egypt. you've gone out to see your people, and you see an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. what does the text say you do first?
options: look this way and that way.
fork.reveal: he looks this way and that way, and sees there is no man. then he strikes the Egyptian. the rabbis still debate what that look meant.

original.note: Hebrew: and he saw. the verb runs through this story and into the next: at the bush, God sees that he turned aside to see.

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses only became a leader at the burning bush.
what it means: before God ever calls him, Moses leaves the palace and looks at his people's suffering.
what a scholar hears: Exodus Rabbah 1:27 on vayar b'sivlotam: he saw their burdens and wept, and shouldered them. 'no man' (2:12) is read both as no witness and as no one else to act.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 2:11 and 2:14.
Exodus Rabbah 1:27 (Moses weeping over their burdens and helping carry them): confirm citation.

Readings of 'he looked this way and that way' (2:12): no witness (plain sense) vs. no one else would act (e.g. Netziv / Exodus Rabbah 1:29 variant readings). Confirm attribution; the script leaves them unattributed.
The killing is described without praise or condemnation; confirm tone.
Moses at the well (2:16–17) extends past the index range (2:11–15) by two verses.
